articles.title_orig: In China’s Taoist martial arts schools, fighting is only part of the lesson
articles.title_zh: In China’s Taoist martial arts schools, fighting is only part of the lesson
articles.content_orig:
SHIYAN, China (AP) — There was a time when Chinese master Yuan Shimao thought martial arts were all about punching and kicking. As a young practitioner, he focused on speed and strength.
"I trained that way for many years without becoming still enough to search within myself," said Yuan, who founded a kung fu academy in central China in 2004.
"But as you gradually settle into stillness, you begin to understand what the scriptures mean by spirit," he added. "You can begin to rediscover yourself."
That process is known as "entering the Dao" in martial arts. It is a guiding principle at Yuan's academy in the sacred Wudang Mountains , where disciplines like kung fu and tai chi draw on Taoist thought.
Practitioners like Yuan start by strengthening the body. As they progress, the mind becomes more resilient and willpower develops.
"The body is a vehicle or vessel within which the spirit resides," Yuan said. "You therefore need a healthy body capable of carrying your spirit."
Yuan began practicing martial arts in the 1980s. Boxing and the Chinese combat sport of sanda attracted him at first.
He heard of Wudang later that decade. As his body ached with rheumatism, Yuan read an article claiming Taoist practices could heal him. So he packed his bags and moved to the mountains. There he became acquainted with Taoist temples and embraced practices such as standing meditation.
He came to understand that movement and stillness are interconnected, rather than opposites. That physical activity can help practitioners quiet the body, allowing them to become calm and grounded.
"I slowly became interested and eventually I benefited from the practice myself," Yuan said. "That process was very profound for me."
Yuan now seeks to share that knowledge with local and foreign students enrolled in the three programs at his academy.
One is a five-year course offering in-depth martial arts training. The second is focused on health and well-being, helping adults exercise and cultivate their minds. The third is a summer camp for children seeking exercise during school breaks.
Chinese philosopher Laozi is believed to have passed on teachings foundational to Taoism to his first student more than 2,500 years ago. That disciple settled on the mountain and helped spread his master's ideas.
"It did not develop into a collective religious faith until after the Qin and Han dynasties," said Shu Chenghai, director of social education at Wudang Museum.
Wudang lay between present-day Xi'an and Luoyang, two major political centers in ancient China. That made it easier for practitioners to seek seclusion while remaining within reach of major population centers.
"The Taoist tradition was therefore never entirely about withdrawing from the world," Shu said.
Wudang's importance as a Taoist religious center came later. During the Tang era, prayers for rain at the mountain were believed to have been answered. Its standing continued to grow under subsequent rulers, reaching its height under Ming emperors.
Guo Xinyi is a Chinese student who began training at Yuan's academy five years ago. She knew of his decades-long commitment to preserving and passing down traditional Taoist martial arts. That made her feel she could trust him.
Within Chinese martial arts, teachers like Yuan are known as "Shifu." The closest English translation is "master." But the Chinese term includes the character for "father." Guo, therefore, thinks of Yuan not merely as a mentor, but as a father figure.
When she first came to his academy, she struggled with conflict with her parents. Her tai chi lessons, though, taught her to approach confrontation calmly.
"I invited Master Yuan to have tea and talk with us," Guo said. "During that conversation, the conflict somehow seemed to dissolve almost invisibly."
Yuan eased her father's anxiety, tension and excessive concern for her, she said, adding that the conversation resembled a tai chi lesson.
"When we encounter conflict, our physical instinct is to resist or attack, to move forward and meet what is coming at us," Guo said. "But tai chi does something different. First, you release tension. Then you sink. Only afterwards do you rise."
The number of students from China and abroad studying at Yuan's academy has increased in recent years.
"In the past, most learners were middle-aged or elderly, but the student population has gradually become younger," he said.
Among that younger generation is Jake Pinnick, an American practitioner who arrived at age 20 and, 16 years later, calls Wudang home.
Pinnick grew up in the U.S. watching kung fu movies and playing sports that relied on competition. What he found in China forever changed his life.
"I came here for martial arts, but I stayed because of this philosophy," said Pinnick, who also became a martial arts master and recently opened his own academy in Wudang.
Yuan said teaching methods have evolved to adapt to younger generations.
Physical training is less demanding and corporal punishment has been eliminated. New ways of motivating students have been introduced instead. Among them is the chanting of slogans aimed at building physical and inner strength.
"Faith in your heart, light in your eyes, and a smile on your face," is one his students' daily chants.
Routines at his academy vary depending on the program, but training can begin as early as 6 a.m. After breakfast, students practice fundamentals before splitting into groups for specific martial arts training. Their schedules also include theory classes and meditation.
Yuan believes learning in Wudang means immersing oneself in the Taoist culture that has shaped its martial arts tradition. That environment, he said, can help students cultivate harmony with nature, with others and within themselves.
"Consider how deeply this nourishes the human heart, mind and spirit," he added. "If practicing martial arts can nourish you to such an extent, what more could you ask for?"
AP video journalist Wu Jia contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Netanyahu says pilot who fought back in Flydubai flight avoided ‘disaster for Israel’
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Netanyahu says pilot who fought back in Flydubai flight avoided ‘disaster for Israel’
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu meets Flydubai passenger who helped subdue pilot in stabbing attack
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has praised the captain of a Flydubai jet as “a true hero” for saving the 174 people aboard after he was stabbed by his co-pilot in what Israeli officials described as an attempt to bring down the plane.
Netanyahu’s comments on Wednesday came as Israel’s government said it would check the identities of all pilots flying into the country, and Flydubai suspended flights to and from Israel while it investigates the episode on Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Netanyahu said the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, “fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker”.
Despite being seriously wounded, he said, Captain Machchhar prevented “a catastrophic mid-air disaster”.
“He is a true hero,” Netanyahu wrote on X.
The Boeing 737 Max 8 made an emergency landing in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia, following the incident. According to Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service, the plane dropped from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in about a minute.
Netanyahu said in a video that most of the passengers were Israeli and that the co-pilot had “apparently intended to bring the aircraft down as it approached Israel”. The co-pilot remains unidentified and the prime minister said Saudi authorities arrested him after the landing and had interrogated him.
A motive for the incident has not been established.
Flydubai, which is owned by the government of Dubai, described the incident as an “altercation in the cockpit” and said that on-duty crew members had “diverted and landed the aircraft safely”. The airline said it was suspending flights to and from Israel while an investigation continued.
The United Arab Emirate’s aviation regulator, the GCAA, said the flight “experienced a security incident that was brought under control”.
Doron Spielman, a spokesman for Netanyahu, said Israel would now vet the identities of all pilots flying into the country.
“Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” he told the Reuters news agency.
United States President Donald Trump said he spoke to Netanyahu about the incident, and was informed that an Israeli plumber intervened to stop the plane from crashing.
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. The pilot “was able to fall back and get the door open and scream.”
“An Israeli plumber saw what was happening,” the US president said. “The plane was going sharply down at an unbelievable angle, so sharp that the rudder ripped off the back of the plane… He ripped this guy out of the seat, threw him back. The crowd got him. The passengers got him, grabbed him. And having never flown aboard a plane, he took the stick, lifted it up and leveled out the plane before it crashed.”
A rescue flight – operated by Flydubai – flew all passengers from Tabuk to their final destination, Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion airport at 15:34 GMT.
Passengers described the episode as a miracle and recounted a frantic struggle to prevent a catastrophe.
Yaniv Hayun, who had entered the cockpit, said he had grabbed the controls and pulled them back, as he had seen done on television, until members of the crew took over.
Netanyahu’s office released a video of the prime minister embracing Hayun at Ben Gurion Airport. Hayun was still wearing the bloodstained shirt he had on during the flight.
Asaf Rajuan, who helped restrain the attacker, spoke with blood still on his forehead.
“This is something you do without thinking, just running to save your daughter’s life, your family’s life,” he said.
Another passenger, Almog Italie, said the plane dropped “very, very sharply,” stabilised, then fell several more times. Naama Bershadski said she closed her eyes and prayed, thinking, “We’re going to die.”
India’s embassy in Riyadh said Captain Machchar, “the brave Indian pilot of Flydubai” has been, “admitted in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia and receiving necessary medical attention”.
The embassy said it was awaiting a full update on the pilot’s health but that “he is reported to be in stable condition”.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI links China’s Moonshot AI to attempt to extract its models’ reasoning
articles.title_zh: OpenAI links China’s Moonshot AI to attempt to extract its models’ reasoning
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said it identified and disrupted a coordinated campaign in which operators attempted to extract protected reasoning from its artificial intelligence models, linking a core cluster of the activity with Chinese startup Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi.
The activity began in early July and later surged to 16,000 requests from more than 4,000 users over two days, OpenAI said. The company ultimately identified related activity across a cluster of more than 15,000 users and said it had fully disrupted the campaign by July 28.
The findings come just weeks after OpenAI rival Anthropic accused several Chinese AI developers, including Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of secretly using its Claude model to help train their own AI systems, underscoring growing concerns among U.S. AI companies that rivals could use their models to develop competing technology more quickly and cheaply.
OpenAI described the latest activity as "adversarial distillation," where one AI model's outputs or reasoning are used to help train or improve another model. The company said extracting such reasoning could allow others to reproduce advanced capabilities without making the same investment in developing and safeguarding frontier models, posing potential safety and national security risks.
The operators did not breach OpenAI's encryption, databases or stored user conversations, according to the company. Instead, they manipulated interactions with its models in an effort to reproduce hidden reasoning in a form visible to the requester.
OpenAI said it was unclear whether all the operators involved were linked to a single actor, but attributed a core cluster of the activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI. The company said it has shared its findings with other AI developers through the Frontier Model Forum as well as government information-sharing channels.
Moonshot did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.title_zh: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.content_orig:
The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June , exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressingâ¦ but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer , affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levelsâ¦ which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

articles.title_orig: Trump hails the US military’s exit from Iraq after 12-year mission against Islamic State
articles.title_zh: Trump hails the US military’s exit from Iraq after 12-year mission against Islamic State
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of September, ending a 23-year presence.
The U.S. military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday.
The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria .
"Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
Soldiers from the U.S.-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the U.S.-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (The Associated Press)
"Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland," Cooper said.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the departure the formal conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and said it marked a transition "from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Pentagon said the U.S. will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi forces even after the withdrawal, while Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga, take the lead in keeping ISIS remnants suppressed.
Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations , according to CENTCOM.
U.S. and coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30. The withdrawal followed an agreement reached between Washington and Baghdad under the Biden administration in 2024 and carried forward under the Trump administration.
Admiral Charles Bradford "Brad" Cooper II, commander of U.S. Central Command, speaks during a joint press conference at CENTCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, on March 5, 2026. (Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images)
Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE
The U.S. has roughly 4,000 troops stationed in Jordan, where American forces will continue monitoring the ISIS threat. Muwaffaq Salti Air Base hosts U.S. combat aircraft and has itself become a target during the conflict with Iran. Three U.S. service members were killed in an Iranian attack on the base in July.
"As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said.
"Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added.
The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.
With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014. (REUTERS/Mohammed Ameen)
For the last several years, roughly 2,500 U.S. troops have been stationed in Iraq. The majority departed last year, leaving hundreds of troops in the northern Kurdish region until the final withdrawal.
The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming.
IRANIAN PRESIDENT BLAMES US FOR MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT WHILE DENYING NUCLEAR AMBITIONS, OFFERS TO DILUTE URANIUM
The Pentagon explicitly identified those militias as one of the security challenges Baghdad will now be expected to confront.
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," Parnell said.
The withdrawal also reduces the number of U.S. military targets inside Iraq after American forces there faced repeated attacks by Iran-aligned groups following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. During this year's war with Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks were killed in Iraq, according to Fox News reporting.
The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats.
Kurdish officials say their region has faced more than 1,000 Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks since the war with Iran began Feb. 28, adding to concerns over the removal of U.S. forces and air-defense capabilities.
Thousands of ISIS fighters also remain in Iraq and Syria despite the collapse of the terror group's organized military threat. The Iraqi government has said its forces will continue operations against ISIS, while the Pentagon said the U.S. remains committed to preventing the group from reconstituting from Iraqi territory.

CENTCOM said U.S. and coalition forces elsewhere in the region will remain prepared to respond if ISIS again poses a threat.
"The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries," Parnell said.

articles.title_orig: Micron Profit, Revenue Surge as Memory Crunch Looks to Last Through 2028
articles.title_zh: Micron Profit, Revenue Surge as Memory Crunch Looks to Last Through 2028
articles.content_orig:
Micron reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Wednesday as the memory maker continues to benefit from soaring demand for AI infrastructure. The stock rose slightly in extended trading.
Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus:
Revenue almost quadrupled in the fiscal fourth quarter from $11.32 billion a year earlier, according to a statement .
For the fiscal first quarter, Micron said it expects revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected $35.40 in adjusted earnings per share on $57 billion in revenue.
Micron's stock has soared more than 500% in the past year, benefiting from a worldwide supply crunch caused by historic levels of demand for memory chips needed for artificial intelligence models and workloads. The shortage has led to a spike in memory costs and resulted in increased prices for  consumer electronics like Apple 's iPads and MacBooks.
Hendi Susanto, portfolio at Gabelli Funds, said in an email after the release that it was "another strong beat and raise for Micron."
"At this point, I have not heard any negative data points pointing to the memory cycle reversing toward a decline anytime soon for the foreseeable future," Susanto wrote.

articles.title_orig: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
articles.title_zh: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
articles.content_orig:
The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for death row inmate Christa Pike to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The justices overturned a last-minute reprieve that was granted by an appeals court on Wednesday morning about an hour before Pike, 50, was due to be put to death.
Tennessee's attorney general had asked the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed the 19-year-old, whom they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, granted Wednesday evening's application to vacate the stay of the execution. No explanation was provided in the order.
The top court's three liberal justices - Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson - dissented.
Sotomayor wrote that the decision cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Pike before her pending legal challenges to her conviction "can be properly considered".
"Tennessee's desire to expedite Pike's execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her 'fundamental interest in [her] own life," she said.
The latest Supreme Court ruling landed just before 18:00 local time. The state's execution order is due to expire at midnight.
If time runs out, the Tennessee Supreme Court would need to set a new execution date, the Associated Press news agency reports.
In a ruling earlier on Wednesday, judges from the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.
Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts had based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.
It was the second time in as many days that the US Supreme Court gave the go-ahead for the convicted murderer's death by lethal injection. On Tuesday, the justices rejected a different appeal from Pike.
Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request this week from the death row inmate.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul had called for the outside review.
Cornell University agreed Wednesday to initiate an independent investigation into how the Ivy League school handled what an unidentified female former student now alleges was fraternity house gang rape , New York Gov. Kathy Hochul told ABC News.
Hochul called for the outside review , saying the allegations raised "serious questions about Cornell campus culture" and whether the university is doing all it can to protect students.
"I wanted to make sure they knew how important this was, and they absolutely agreed. And they're acting on this this afternoon. So, they'll be reporting on what the details are, but they will be conducting what I asked for, which is an independent outside investigation of what happened," Hochul told ABC News on Wednesday.
"People need to know the truth and I think it's important for the public, for the victim, her family and the university community to know that their university did everything that they're supposed to do," she said.
Cornell's internal data show 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing sexual assault during their time on campus, but Hochul said the problem was acute on every campus.
"There's been a culture of this kind of treatment of young women on campuses for as long as I've been in college, and it has to change," Hochul said.
Cornell confirmed the outside investigation on Wednesday but has not yet provided details.
Prosecutors in central New York this week announced that they are reopening the investigation of the alleged sexual assault after a former Cornell student filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged, assaulted and gang raped by seven former and current members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell, sparking outrage about the incident.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering whether to bring criminal charges related to the incident, though he said the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" than the woman's statement to police two years ago.

Cornell's Chi Phi chapter is barred from campus. Trey Robb, the interim executive director of Chi Phi fraternity, said in a statement that all the accused members were kicked out of the Cornell chapter within three days of Jane Doe filing her police report in 2024.
Three of the defendants named in the suit have denied the allegations through their attorneys.
"Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said in a statement Monday, in part.

articles.title_orig: Trump unveils $200 billion South Korean investment in US; Seoul hedges on Alaska pipeline
articles.title_zh: Trump unveils $200 billion South Korean investment in US; Seoul hedges on Alaska pipeline
articles.content_orig:
President Trump announced plans Wednesday for South Korea to invest in exporting natural gas from Alaska, a project long backed by Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is in a competitive reelection contest there.
It marks the second time in three days that the president has sought to highlight planned foreign investments in states where Republican Senate candidates are in tight election campaigns. Mr. Trump made a similar Oval Office announcement on Monday for a massive steel plant in Iowa, another state where Republicans are defending a Senate seat.
The project consists of an 807-mile natural gas pipeline connecting Alaska's petroleum-rich North Slope to a liquefied natural gas export terminal in southern Alaska. It will eventually reduce energy costs for the state's residents by providing a reliable and secure supply, the White House said. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said liquefied natural gas could also be exported to Asia.
Officials said during the Oval Office event that building the pipeline will take three years and that exports of liquefied natural gas would begin two years after that — but that was dependent on financing coming through fully.
It was not clear how quickly South Korea's government would approve the project and how much it planned to spend.
The pipeline is part of a series of projects that Mr. Trump said would get nearly $200 billion in South Korean funds, including a power plant in Texas and eight "large-scale" nuclear power plants. Further details on those investments are not clear.
The investment comes from pledges made as part of a 2025 trade deal with South Korea, which included promises of $350 billion in investments in the United States in exchange for lower U.S. tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products.
Mr. Trump credited his controversial tariff strategy for making the announcement possible, saying, "Our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars."
The president credited Sullivan during the Oval Office event.
"He's got my ear, and he's had my ear for a long time on Alaska," Mr. Trump said. The president added that "all these energy projects are all mine, and I got 'em done working with Dan Sullivan."
Sullivan said, "the sky is the limit when we get this project done."
"Mr. President, this one is huge for Alaska," Sullivan said, adding that he'd been working on it "relentlessly."
The push to deliver big projects in areas where GOP candidates could use a boost comes as Mr. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to nearly historic lows ahead of midterm elections. Republicans are also contending with voters' historical tendency to reject whichever party controls the White House during the midterms.
Even Mr. Trump himself has begun acknowledging that Republicans could face an uphill climb in their push to retain control of both chambers of Congress after November, but suggests it is because his administration hasn't done enough to promote its accomplishments.
"I've done a very bad job of explaining," the president said during an event in the White House's East Room, which came before the subsequent announcement on the Alaska investment.
He's promised to help rectify that by spending much of the next 30 days on the road, campaigning ahead of the midterms — though he is beginning that swing with trips to Texas, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, which are all normally solidly red states.
Sullivan, who has been a persistent advocate for the Alaska natural gas project and has encouraged South Korean investment, is a two-term senator facing a competitive challenge from Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
Wednesday's Alaska event came two days after Mr. Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel plant to be built in Iowa by a Minnesota company owned by an Indian industrial conglomerate.
In Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is in a close U.S. Senate contest with Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the seat being vacated by retiring two-term Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson spoke in the Oval Office during the announcement.
Alaska and Iowa — where Mr. Trump won comfortably each time he has run for president — are among the states where Democrats are targeting Republican-held Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections, less than five weeks away.
Democrats need to gain a net of four seats in the 100-member Senate to overtake Republicans in the majority.

articles.title_orig: Judge allows Paramount to close $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery
articles.title_zh: Judge allows Paramount to close $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery
articles.content_orig:
A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
Judge clears way for Paramount to acquire Warner Bros.
The seismic merger will bring together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+, and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
Shortly after the judge’s approval, David Ellison, the CEO and controlling shareholder of Paramount Skydance, announced that Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz would become co-CEO of the combined media giant.
Kreiz will join the company Oct. 5, and the companies said in a statement the deal “is expected to close on October 6.”
“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.
Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.
After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department , the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s Democratic attorney general, Rob Bonta.
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potentially imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.
Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21 , which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close ally of President Donald Trump’s. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.
After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News. She has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence .
The merged company pledged to invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called ticking fee kicks in for Paramount Skydance.
In order to build confidence in the merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.
“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
A spokesperson for the California Department of Justice said Wednesday that they are “pleased the court has approved our settlement.”
“Our settlement with Paramount resolves our antitrust concerns in every market we brought in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and centers the needs, concerns, and futures of California workers,” the spokesperson said.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the Block the Merger coalition , urged in an amicus brief that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.
The group criticized the state attorneys general for what it called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld,” the group said.
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.
Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

A year after his explosive tenure at Doge, the SpaceX CEO is back in the Trump administration’s good graces
Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
after newsletter promotion
Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release.
“We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”
Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare.
Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

articles.content_orig:
Alphabet unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on Wednesday, its most advanced artificial intelligence model yet, offering major improvements in coding, cybersecurity, and complex professional work.
The company said the model sets a new record in real-world software engineering, ties for first in cybersecurity, and leads another benchmark measuring performance across finance, legal, and other professional tasks.
Argon is already being used internally to optimize memory at Google's data centers, freeing up hundreds of terabytes of memory without buying additional hardware, the company said. Quantum computing researchers have also utilized the model.
Google plans to launch the new model in phases, starting with trusted cybersecurity partners while working with the U.S. government on pre-release safety evaluations.
"Starting this rollout in this way gives us more confidence, but also enables us to put a model that is trained and strong in cyber defense in the hands of defenders as soon as possible," Tulsee Doshi, Google's Gemini model product lead, told CNBC.
The model release comes a day after CEO Sundar Pichai signed a voluntary agreement with President Donald Trump and major tech executives at the White House, following a luncheon to address rising AI safety concerns.
Gemini 4 also launches nearly a year after Gemini 3 put the tech company back at the forefront of the heated AI model race. The long-awaited model represents a major push at the frontier and follows Google's pivot toward scaling faster, lower-cost flash models.
Google on Wednesday said it's looking to scale safeguards in four key cybersecurity areas, including misuse and prompt injection, before launching publicly.
Doshi referred to Gemini 4 as an "incredibly well-rounded" model that excels at running long, multi-step tasks. The new model also represents a meaningful cybersecurity step up from Google's 3.8 Flash Cyber model released earlier this month , outperforming in vulnerability discovery.
"We really believe that a model of this caliber and this level of frontier performance is meaningfully important for defenders," Doshi said.
Argon ties with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Grok 4.7 on cybersecurity benchmarks and ahead of GPT-6 Astra and recent Anthropic models on the Vals Index.

Legislation to permanently ban the sale of Chinese vehicles in the United States stalled out on Wednesday as senators struggled to seal an agreement, virtually guaranteeing that the bill will have to wait until after the November elections.
The bipartisan bill, sponsored by Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio and Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, aims to prevent China’s auto industry from gaining a foothold in the U.S. market. It would ban the import, manufacture and sale of internet-connected vehicles, software and hardware linked to China or other foreign adversaries, including Russia and North Korea.
Chinese automakers are already effectively banned from selling or building vehicles in the U.S. under a policy put into place by the Biden administration, but senators are hoping to more permanently shut the door.
The summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Washington last week, which focused in part on trade between the world’s two largest economies, had given the legislation renewed momentum. Slotkin said nearly every senator was prepared to support it, and they had initially planned to seek passage last week without a formal roll call vote.
Senators delayed action to continue negotiations with the lone holdout, Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who argued the legislation could unfairly sweep in Mercedes-Benz. The bill would bar vehicles made by companies with more than a 15% ownership stake from Chinese entities. Mercedes-Benz has nearly 20% passive Chinese ownership.
Supporters say they will try again after the elections. But the delay is a setback for bipartisan legislation that has drawn support from automakers and labor unions as Washington grapples with the growing global reach of China’s auto industry — and concerns about potential surveillance technology.
“It is literally a driving spy machine on wheels,” Slotkin said of Chinese vehicles. “All of that data and all of that information goes back to Beijing.”
Lawmakers see threat from Chinese EVs
Lawmakers and analysts have warned of dire consequences if Chinese EVs should become available in the U.S.
“I am concerned about what can happen to the U.S. automobile industry with the Chinese electric vehicles,” said Republican Sen. Steve Daines in an interview with The Associated Press before the Trump-Xi summit. “They are remarkable, high quality at a much lower cost. But it’s not fair if you have a product that is significantly subsidized by a government to be able to come into our market."
Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly overseas, competing aggressively on price and technology and putting pressure on established manufacturers in Europe and other markets. In the first eight months of this year, China’s exports of new-energy vehicles more than doubled from the previous year, shipping out more than 3.4 million vehicles, according to China Association of Automobile Manufactures.
Chinese automakers supplied 60% of global electric car sales in 2025, while European and North American automakers were each responsible for about 15% of global sales, according to IEA, or the International Energy Agency.
Their emergence has raised concerns in Detroit that allowing them into the U.S. could expose domestic automakers to a new source of lower-cost competition.
Trump, however, has at times taken a more welcoming approach to Chinese investment in the U.S. auto industry. Speaking at the Detroit Economic Club in January, he said he was open to Chinese automakers building factories in the United States as long as they employed American workers.
“If they want to come in and build the plant and hire you and hire your friends and your neighbors, that’s great. I love that,” Trump said. “Let China come in.”
That position has put Trump at odds with an unusual coalition of lawmakers, automakers and labor unions that has pushed to keep Chinese vehicles out of the U.S. market.
In April 2026, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said “no” when he was asked if Chinese EV makers such as BYD would come and set up joint ventures in the U.S.
But in early September, before he hosted China's Xi, Trump again said he would not oppose Chinese automakers building ​cars in the United States.
The White House didn’t respond to a request by AP regarding its stance on the bill.
Slotkin and Moreno have framed their legislation around two threats: protecting the U.S. auto industry from heavily subsidized Chinese competitors and preventing technology embedded in connected vehicles from collecting sensitive data on Americans.
In July, Slotkin called Chinese cars “surveillance packages on wheels,” arguing that they could collect information on American drivers and sensitive sites and transmit it to Beijing. Moreno has said China’s auto industry “was built to destroy American manufacturing, gut the middle class, and undermine our national security.”
The bill would prohibit the import, manufacture, sale, resale or introduction into interstate commerce of connected vehicles and related software and hardware associated with China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. It would effectively write into law and expand restrictions that began under the Biden administration, making it harder for a future administration to reverse them.
But some are concerned that the 15% ownership cap could hurt companies with strong roots in the United States.
“We're not going to have the president of the United States sign a bill — nor would he — that bans Mercedes-Benz from the United States of America,” said Moreno, also mentioning companies like Volvo. “We have to figure out a way to manage all of that.”
James Lewis, a distinguished fellow with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said the bill could return after the midterm elections, given the threat that Chinese carmakers pose to U.S. companies.
“China can make enough cars in a single year to supply the entire global demand. You don’t need any other countries to make cars with China in the picture,” Lewis said. “This is existential for the car companies.”
“Car companies care a lot. They’re very influential,” he said. “They’re deeply concerned about this.”

articles.title_orig: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, Israel says, after co-pilot stabs pilot
articles.title_zh: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, Israel says, after co-pilot stabs pilot
articles.content_orig:
A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent attempt by one of the pilots to seize control of the aircraft and crash it, passengers and Israeli officials said.
"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers and other crew members who intervened. The prime minister said he instructed Israel's "security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats."
An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack, which was thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist, and with their own hands returned control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew that was present," according to a statement.
The plane diverted to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base. No passengers were injured in the incident, but the pilot who was attacked by his fellow crew member reportedly sustained stab wounds, and Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
According to Netanyahu, the pilot who carried out the stabbing was placed under arrest and was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities." An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship.
In a social media post , the Israel Foreign Ministry identified the wounded pilot as Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. It described him as a "hero" who "fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit."
According to the foreign ministry, Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door to allow passengers and crew to enter and intervene.
"Together, their extraordinary courage saved 174 lives," the foreign ministry said.
The plane landed in Tel Aviv shortly before 8 p.m. local time on Wednesday. People could be heard singing and chanting as the passengers disembarked. Family members came to the airport to celebrate their loved ones' safe return.
One passenger said the plane dropped "very, very sharply suddenly" multiple times before balancing out. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."
"There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," Ohayon said.
Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
One passenger seated at the front of the plane said a "group of young people fought" with the attacker.
The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information. CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.
The Israeli Air Force was first to notice something was wrong, an Israeli official with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News. The air force noticed the flight deviating from its flight path and descending at an alarming rate, the official said. When it tried to contact the plane, it received no response. It then got the emergency alert that specified a hijacking, not just a distress call.
At that point, according to the official, the flight was still several hundred miles from Israeli airspace. However, even 90 seconds or so into the incident, the air force feared a 9/11-style attack, so it immediately made the decision to close Israeli airspace, and seconds after that it scrambled several jets, the official said.
The jets never left Israeli airspace because it became clear that the plane had turned toward Saudi Arabia, and that Saudi Arabia had scrambled its own jets, the official said.
This sequence of events occurred within the span of about two to three minutes, according to the official, and the entire episode lasted about 15 minutes.
A statement from FlyDubai said only that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and that the aircraft "was successfully secured by on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely" in Saudi Arabia.
The airline said "all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for," and it confirmed that two replacement aircraft had been deployed to Tabuk to "relieve the passengers and crew," though many Israeli passengers told media outlets they would not reboard a FlyDubai plane.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the airline said in its statement, urging "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that there were four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship aboard the flight.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.
Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.
Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."
Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in the upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X : "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."
"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday , saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."
"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

articles.title_orig: FCC head says government-funded Trump ads are ‘normal’ and ‘don’t raise any red flags’
articles.title_zh: FCC head says government-funded Trump ads are ‘normal’ and ‘don’t raise any red flags’
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Supreme Court rules Tennessee can execute lone woman on death row
Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday that new pro-Trump TV ads paid for with government funds don’t “merit any sort of FCC review.”
“It doesn’t strike me as anything at all out of the ordinary,” Carr said of the ads, which have aired across the country in recent weeks.
Asked about allegations that the ads are “propaganda,” Carr laughed.
The White House has “explained that these are just normal-course public service announcements, PSAs, that you see all the time. I don’t think there’s anything unique or different about it,” he said at a news conference .
“There’s nothing in there that strikes me that merit any sort of FCC review,” said Carr, whom Trump appointed to the agency.
A reporter pointed out that the progressive advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC noting that the Trump campaign used one of the ads in 2024.
Carr brushed off the concern, telling reporters that “there’s groups on the left that have, you know, long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process” but that the ads “don’t raise any red flags.”
Public Citizen did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC, told NBC News in a statement, “I recognize the concern shared by others that taxpayer dollars are being used to promote a political message, particularly given the timing of these ads coming so close to an election.”
“While it is not surprising to see the FCC exercise a double standard when it comes to its investigative decisions, I am certain we will hear more about this from folks in Congress, who are ultimately responsible,” her statement said.
The use of federal funds to pay for the ads has drawn bipartisan criticism , with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., saying they “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., calling them an “absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like.”
Trump defended the ads when asked about them Wednesday in the Oval Office.
“I’m not running for office and I don’t talk about anybody,” he said. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.”
“Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country,” he added.
The first of the ads features Trump describing how he wants to “defeat communism” while the song “ Love Me ” by JMSN plays in the background.
Another spot is a slightly shorter version of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, which shows him walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voice-over to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”
In its complaint Tuesday, Public Citizen said that the messages are thinly veiled campaign ads timed to motivate Trump’s supporters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and that they are unlawful.
“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising. Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads,” the complaint says, adding that none of the ads to date “meet the standard of a public service announcement.”
“They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program,” the complaint says.
Carr has made headlines for using his post to go after late-night comedians like Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and network programs that he has alleged have liberal biases.
The FCC issued an order this year directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated television stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule after the White House and ABC clashed over a joke Kimmel made about first lady Melania Trump.
Disney is challenging the review with a suit alleging the FCC is seeking to coerce and retaliate against “a network that refuses to bow to the ⁠administration’s ​demands.” Carr has said the ABC license review stems from the FCC’s probe of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices — not “speech.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Leaning into culture war flashpoints, Hegseth says he has transformed U.S. military
articles.title_zh: Leaning into culture war flashpoints, Hegseth says he has transformed U.S. military
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Wednesday in Quantico, Va. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
At a gathering at U.S. Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told hundreds of junior military officers and enlisted leaders that the Trump administration has achieved a cultural shift in the military.
"No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors," Hegseth said on Wednesday. "The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in, with testosterone testing on top."
Hegseth has vowed to shrink what he says is a bloated flag-officer corps since he took over at the Pentagon. He said he'd already achieved a 10% reduction and aimed to reach 20%. But his firings so far, and the unconventional way he has reached down into promotion boards to essentially end the careers of some senior officers, has drawn bipartisan criticism. Many of the notable firings were of Black or female officers, let go without explanation despite excellent service records.
Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, issued this statement:
"Throughout his tenure, Secretary Hegseth has taken countless reckless, partisan actions that have damaged our military. He has ended the careers of dozens of our most accomplished senior officers and refused to explain why. Today's news should alarm every American."
In his speech, Hegseth defended his policies and claimed that retention and recruitment, including among women and minorities, has risen. He called the new force "color-blind" and merit-based. Hegseth took considerable time to rail against the media for reporting on troop morale and depleted munitions stocks in the war with Iran.
"A free press is, of course, important, but partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually," he said.
Despite the war in Iran, now in its seventh month, the Pentagon hasn't held a news briefing since May, even with a handpicked press corps more sympathetic to the Trump administration.
The event echoed a gathering last year where Hegseth delivered an unusually partisan speech to hundreds of generals and admirals, despite the U.S. military's foundational tradition of avoiding politics. The flag officers stayed almost completely silent as Hegseth spoke about culture war issues mentioned in his book The War on Warriors . He said that the "State of the Force" address would be an annual event, and was no less partisan this year, blaming past generals and defense secretaries by name for weakening the military.
Hegseth also announced new initiatives around autonomous weapons, technological innovation, base construction and domestic production of essential military supplies.
He pledged to elevate the military's chaplains and called religious faith the most essential component of our republic.
This week Hegseth also announced an end to civilian tenured positions at U.S. military academies, which a Pentagon press release said would "reform our educational institutions to ensure they remain laser-focused on lethality and readiness."
While criticizing elite academic institutions as anti-American in his speech, Hegseth named five new colleges that will pilot an enhanced relationship with the Pentagon to produce officer candidates.

articles.title_orig: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.title_zh: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee can carry out its planned execution of the lone woman on death row after the Supreme Court vacated a lower court’s Wednesday morning order that had temporarily blocked the move.
The high court’s decision hours later caps a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering in a bid by convicted murderer Christa Pike’s legal team to spare her life. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
About an hour before her scheduled execution at 10 a.m. local time in Nashville, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth District said it needed to review claims made by her lawyers. At issue was whether Pike can reopen a court proceeding centered around her allegations that she was sexually abused beginning when she was a child — abuse that the state did not dispute at a special hearing in August.
The appeals court in a split decision agreed to a “short” reprieve halting her execution “in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”
In turn, the state attorney general’s office asked the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that the execution must go on to “avoid rewarding Pike’s abusive delay tactics.”
Both Gov. Bill Lee and the Supreme Court had said this week they would not stop Pike’s execution.
Before learning Monday that Lee would not be intervening in her case, Pike, 50, wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser: “Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace.”
“I am not afraid to die,” wrote Pike, who has been on death row for more than three decades. “I’m only nervous about the process.”
If executed, Pike would be the first woman in more than 200 years that the state puts to death, according to historical records .
In 1995, Pike was 18 when Knoxville police say she and two teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19. Police say Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike doesn’t dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They had asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, will likely create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state hasn’t denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court appeared to be Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.” The high court denied her petition Tuesday evening.
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken” that the governor would not be granting clemency.
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
In her letter, Pike wrote that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also point to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time. Tadaryl Shipp received a life sentence because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and received probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention. Pike’s lawyers say that her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers say that her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed into solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, was asked by Pike’s lawyers to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider if any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse. Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. But, she added, Pike’s case is a lesson of the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.
May Martinez is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.
Martinez recalled how, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts weren’t buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. Xavier Becerra probably hates his new nickname, which is why Steve Hilton is hoping it sticks.
Hilton’s campaign turned a reported White House insult from 2024 into a campaign attack ahead of Wednesday night’s CNN debate , as the Republican gubernatorial candidate created a website branding his Democratic opponent “Bitch–ass Becerra.”
Former White House adviser Susan Rice dissed Becerra with the moniker during their time working in the Biden administration. The new website attacks Becerra’s leadership as California attorney general and US health secretary, drawing heavily on reported criticism from Democrats who worked alongside him.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The California Post reported Tuesday that former Biden administration colleagues questioned Becerra’s fitness to be governor, with one alleging he disparaged migrant children as “little Juanitos and Juanitas.”
“I do not think he is qualified to be the governor,” Becerra’s ex-colleague told The Post.
“I don’t think he’s qualified to be the boss of anything.”
Becerra was alo described as having “dead-fish eyes” during an emotional meeting about migrant children in crowded detention facilities.
“No emotion. No response. Nothing there,” the official said.
Becerra’s campaign called the allegation about his remarks on migrant children “an outright fabrication,” and spokesperson Jonathan Underland dismissed former colleagues’ criticism as “jealousy.”
Hilton’s website depicts Becerra wearing a jacket plastered with corporate and union logos, including Chevron, Pacific Gas & Electric and the California Teachers Association.
“Chaos. Fraud. Child trafficking. Gender extremism. Higher costs for you,” the site says. “Empty Suit Becerra stood by and did nothing. He enabled it all.”

In a previous interview, Hilton told The Post that Becerra lacked the mental acuity to serve as governor.

Sections accuse him of weakening safeguards for migrant children, presiding over fraud and contributing to higher gas and electricity bills. One heading declares: “Even Democrats ripped Becerra.”
Among them is former Biden administration official Xochitl Hinojosa, whose criticism during a CNN appearance in May stunned other Democrats.
“I don’t think that he will be able to stand up to Trump and lead,” Hinojosa said.

Axios reported in 2024 that Rice called Becerra “bitch-ass” and “idiot.”A spokesperson for Rice ‘categorically’ denied the reporting about her relationship with Becerra and Vice President Kamala Harris.
The Post’s most recent report quoted an ex-Biden official saying Rice berated Becerra during meetings about the migrant crisis “at least once a week.”
Becerra also was getting burned on social media this week for an awkward interview with the San Francisco Standard’s comedy correspondent, Sophia Garrow , who asked him to name companies whose donations he would reject.
Becerra, who is seeking to follow in Gov. Gavin Newsom’s lofty fundraising footsteps , left open the door to accept money from Purdue Pharma, which he had sued over its role in the opioid crisis, saying he believed in “redemption” for companies.
Garrow repeatedly used the name “David” when talking about San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, echoing an error on Becerra’s endorsement page. Becerra did not correct her.
“What’s your relationship like with David?” she asked.
“Growing,” Becerra replied, without correcting the name. “He’s done a number of important things, amazing things.”
Becerra held a substantial lead heading into the campaign’s only debate, with a recent PPIC poll having him at 60% to Hilton’s 38%.
